goldens.comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:123 — [P2, confidence 100] "UserCredentialModel recoveryCodesCredential = new UserCredentialModel(\"\", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson);" When a user-storage update succeeds, this boundary discards the generated timestamp and user label, so the provider cannot reproduce the configured recovery credential metadata.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that when creating UserCredentialModel for user storage update, the code passes empty string for id and only type/recoveryCodesJson, but does not include the timestamp (createdDate) or userLabel from the credentialModel. Looking at the diff, the credentialModel parameter contains this metadata (it's a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel), but the UserCredentialModel constructor only receives type and challengeResponse. This means when userStorage.updateCredential succeeds, the storage provider receives incomplete metadata. The BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage test provider shows it expects to set createdDate from Time.currentTimeMillis() itself, but the original credentialModel's timestamp and label are lost.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/servers/auth-server/services/testsuite-providers/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:340 — [P2, confidence 100] "return generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()));" A successful recovery-code validation never removes or marks the code in `recoveryCodes`, so each subsequent read reconstructs the full unused set and recovery-code exhaustion never reaches its regeneration transition.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(), when validating recovery codes (lines 283-305), the code only checks if the input matches any code in the stored list using `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. However, there is no code to remove or mark the used code from `myUser.recoveryCodes`. This means the same recovery code can be used multiple times, and the exhaustion logic (which should trigger regeneration when all codes are used) will never be reached. This is a real bug in the test provider implementation that affects the recovery code functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/servers/auth-server/services/testsuite-providers/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:340 — [P1, confidence 100] "return generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()));" A federated recovery code is never consumed, so the same recovery code authorizes every subsequent login.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is correct. Looking at the `isValid` method in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java around line 340, when validating recovery codes, the code only checks if the input matches any of the stored codes using `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. However, unlike the OTP credential handling which stores state, there is no code to consume/remove the used recovery code from `myUser.recoveryCodes` after successful validation. Recovery codes are designed to be single-use, but this implementation allows the same code to be reused indefinitely. This is a security bug in the test user storage provider.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` at line 218 only checks `if (isOTPType(credentialType))` to add OTP to disableable types, but does not include a check for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`. Since the diff adds support for recovery codes credentials (as seen in `supportsCredentialType`, `updateCredential`, `isConfiguredFor`, and `isValid` methods), the `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` method should also be updated to allow disabling recovery codes. Without this, users cannot disable/remove their recovery codes credential through the normal credential management flow.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff at line 197, when creating a recovery codes credential in updateCredential(), the code sets recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse()) but never calls setUserLabel(). Comparing this to the OTP credential creation above (lines 176-189), the OTP also doesn't set a user label, but the issue is that when getCredentials() reconstructs the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel (lines 230-243), it passes myUser.recoveryCodes.getUserLabel() to createFromValues(), which will always be null since it was never set. This means any user label that might have been intended to be stored is lost. The finding correctly identifies that the user label is discarded during the federated storage update.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/servers/auth-server/services/testsuite-providers/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:244 — [P2, confidence 75] "log.error(\"Could not deserialize  credential of type: recovery-codes\");" A recovery-code record whose persisted JSON cannot be decoded is logged and omitted from the federated credential stream while still counted as configured, causing its recovery-code authentication path to have no usable credential rather than surfacing a recoverable migration failure.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real inconsistency in the code. In getCredentials() (line 227-244), when JSON deserialization fails, the error is logged but the credential is silently omitted from the returned stream. However, in isConfiguredFor() (line 274-276), the code checks `myUser.recoveryCodes != null` without verifying if the credential data is valid/deserializable. This means a user could have `isConfiguredFor()` return true for recovery codes, but `getCredentials()` would return an empty stream for that credential type, causing authentication to fail in a confusing way rather than surfacing the underlying data corruption issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:123 — [P2, confidence 100] "UserCredentialModel recoveryCodesCredential = new UserCredentialModel(\"\", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson);" The user-storage path persists the generated recovery codes as raw JSON instead of the hashed recovery credential, so anyone who obtains that storage record can use the codes to bypass MFA until they are consumed or replaced.

adjudication.rationale: The finding misunderstands the code flow. Looking at the diff, the raw codes JSON is passed to `updateCredential` for user storage, but this is intentional - the user storage provider (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage) receives the raw codes and stores them in its own format. The local storage path uses `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential()` which properly hashes the codes via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel. The user storage is responsible for its own credential handling - this is the expected pattern for federated user storage where Keycloak delegates credential management to external systems. The test code in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage shows it stores and validates these codes appropriately for testing purposes.

This is a valid concern about incomplete test coverage for newly added logic.
